newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Peng Zhen - purge victim who returned to power.
newsitem.headline: China's Peng Zhen - purge victim who returned to power.

text.p: Peng Zhen, who died on Saturday, was the first senior Chinese leader to fall victim to the Cultural Revolution but survived 12 years in disgrace and returned to play an influential role in the post-Mao reforms.
His death removed the highest ranking survivor of the generation of Communist revolutionaries who swept to power in 1949.

Chosen by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping as head of parliament, he oversaw the establishment of system of law to replace a centuries-old vacuum that both leaders blamed for the chaos of Chairman Mao Zedong's 1966-76 Cultural Revolution.

Born in 1902, he wielded enormous power behind the scenes long after leaving his official posts. Well into his 90s he still appeared occasionally in public, sometimes in a wheelchair, lively, alert and a force to be reckoned with.
He commanded a vast network of connections built up after years in the party hierarchy and as chairman of parliament, the National People's Congress.
He stepped down from that post in April 1988 as part of Deng's drive to retire ageing communist comrades, but retained widespread influence.

He was a staunch ally of Deng, and a particularly vociferous promoter of Deng's campaign against "bourgeois liberalisation" -- Chinese jargon for Western ideas -- launched during a hard-line resurgence in early 1987.
He was once described by an adversary as "disarmingly aggressive".
But later that year, he was dropped from the Communist Party's Central Committee, and his removal essentially barred him from ever reaching the highest rungs of Chinese politics.
Still, Peng was always consulted on major policy as an elder statesman who had a wide-ranging web of friends and followers.

During the 1989 pro-democracy movement that sent millions of Chinese into the streets, Peng reportedly defended the Beijing leadership's decision to impose martial law. However, he appeared to take a less harsh line than his ageing colleagues against the students who demonstrated.
The motives of the students, he was reported as telling a special emergency meeting of the party Central Committee, were pure and patriotic.
Days later, Beijing leaders ordered troops and tanks to crack down on the protests, killing hundreds.
In the 1980s, Peng spearheaded Deng's drive to restore the rule of law after the chaos of the extreme left-wing Cultural Revolution.
He was the first member of the party's politburo to be purged in that upheaval.

Communist Party secretary and mayor of Beijing for 15 years and a close ally of then head of state Liu Shaoqi, Peng was hounded from office in June, 1966, by radicals charging he had transformed Beijing into a personal empire from which to combat Mao's policies.

He returned to prominence in the late 1970s along with long-time ally, Deng, and was appointed chairman of the National People's Congress in 1983, a job that afforded him ample opportunity to build a power base.
In 1979, Peng was named to head a legal commission set up by the parliament to help it to strengthen China's battered legal system and "guarantee the People's democracy".
Born into a poor peasant family in northern Shanxi province, Peng Zhen joined the Communist Party in 1923.
Building a reputation as a good organiser, he was elected to the Party Central Committee in 1945 and in 1964 was described officially as one of Mao's "close comrades in arms".

But in 1965 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution and Peng, who had allowed publication in Beijing of some criticism, was banished to the countryside for 12 years. He returned to Beijing only after Deng returned to power in 1978.

Even after his retirement, he clung to such honorary posts as president of the China Mayors' Association, and president of the Society for Study of Huang He (Yellow River) Cultural and Economic Development.
